strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated scalability bottleneck in differentiable optimization layers: the cost of KKT-based implicit differentiation. The proposed active-set ('ghost') Lagrangian reduction is a clean idea that converts inequality-constrained lower-level problems into equality-constrained surrogates, enabling the near-constant O(log(1/eps)) hypergradient oracle of Kornowski et al. (2024) to apply beyond equality-only settings.

The theoretical contribution is meaningful: Theorem 4.6 improves the hypergradient approximation cost from O~(eps^-1) (Kornowski et al., 2024, Thm 5.3) to O(log(1/eps)), and Corollary 4.7 yields the best-known O~(delta^-1 eps^-3) Goldstein-stationarity rate for linearly constrained bilevel optimization. Appendix F is a nice touch, providing both an impossibility-style argument for why the active-set assumption is needed (Lemma F.1, via a 1-D example) and a smoothed variant (Theorem F.2) that avoids the assumption.

The solver-agnostic reformulation (Section 5, Lemma E.1), replacing the upper-level objective perturbation by a linear term c^T y with c = detach(grad_y f), is practically important and is what makes the drop-in, black-box-solver design possible.

The implementation is released as an open-source PyTorch library with a CvxpyLayer-compatible interface, and the empirical evaluation covers several baselines (CvxpyLayer, QPTH, LPGD, BPQP, dQP), multiple tasks (synthetic DFL, Sudoku, SOCP), scaling ablations in problem dimension, memory profiling, gradient-accuracy checks (cosine similarity to a reference exact gradient), and tolerance/batch-size sensitivity studies. The convergence results show the approximate gradients do not hurt training.
weaknesses: The assumptions are strong and substantially limit applicability: strong convexity of the lower level, LICQ, correct active-set identification, and a locally constant active set (Assumptions 4.2-4.3). Degenerate or near-degenerate multipliers (lambda* ~ 0 on active constraints), which are common in practice, fall outside the theory, and the method's behavior in such regimes is not analyzed. Appendix D.1's own hardness example (F(x) = sqrt(1-x^2)) shows how fragile the general convex-constraint setting is.

The generalization to general convex constraints (Appendix D) is weaker than advertised: Assumption D.1 requires an oracle returning eps-accurate primal-dual solutions that share the optimal active set, and the authors admit no known algorithm achieves this for the dual. The 'extension' is thus largely a conditional reduction under an assumed oracle rather than a complete algorithmic contribution.

Several proofs are terse or hand-wavy. Theorem B.1's proof reduces to comparing two KKT systems (Eqs. 14-15) that differ by a diag(1, lambda*_I) factor and dismisses the step as 'simple linear algebra' without details; Theorem C.2 asserts delta-close solutions 'in O~(1) time' for 'well-conditioned' problems without justification; Lemma A.3's stated bound appears dimensionally inconsistent; Theorem F.2's statement (expectation over a smoothed objective with a dist(0, partial-delta) term) and proof sketch are informal and hard to verify.

Experiments are confined to synthetic/medium-scale tasks (dy up to ~1000, simple MLPs) on CPU; no real-world decision-focused learning benchmarks (e.g., portfolio, energy scheduling, shortest-path) are included. One baseline (BPQP) is re-implemented by the authors, and Alt-Diff is excluded for being 'too slow', which weakens the comprehensiveness of comparisons. There is also an internal inconsistency: Section 6 states all methods run on CPU, while Appendix G.2/Figure 7 reports 'peak GPU memory' (and 'GD' appears to be a typo).

Some claims are overstated relative to prior work: LPGD is already first-order and solver-agnostic, so the 'first method to combine all properties' claim hinges mainly on the finite-time hypergradient guarantee. Table 1's 'Exact hypergradient' column, where the proposed method is marked with a dagger meaning approximate, is a confusing presentation choice.

Presentation issues: the source-code URL in the abstract is missing; duplicate references (Zhang et al. 2020a/b are the same paper; Maclaurin et al. 2015a/b); various typos and grammatical slips; Figure 6's memory axis (up to 500 GB for CPU runs) looks implausible and needs clarification.

The practical mechanism for active-set identification (how multipliers from black-box solvers are thresholded, and what happens when identification fails) is not described, which affects reproducibility of the central algorithmic step.

strengths: The core idea is attractive and well-motivated: replacing expensive KKT/Hessian-based implicit differentiation with an active-set Lagrangian 'ghost' bilevel reformulation that yields an epsilon-approximate hypergradient using only first-order information, addressing a gap explicitly noted by Kornowski et al. (2024) (equality-only formulations admit O(log(1/epsilon)) hypergradient approximation while penalty-based handling of inequalities costs O(epsilon^-1)).

The solver-agnostic reformulation (Section 5, Equation 6-7) that replaces the upper-level objective with a linear surrogate c^T y (with c = detach(grad_y f)) so that the perturbed lower-level problem can be solved by a black-box solver is a clever and practically valuable engineering contribution, enabling use of GUROBI/MOSEK without solver-specific backward passes.

The paper is honest about the strength of Assumption 4.3 (active-set identification) and devotes Appendix F to arguing its necessity (Lemma F.1) plus a smoothed fallback (Theorem F.2), which is a fair treatment of a key limitation.

The library targets drop-in compatibility with CvxpyLayer and evaluates against a reasonable set of baselines (CvxpyLayer, QPTH, LPGD, BPQP, dQP), with ablations on memory, tolerance sensitivity, gradient cosine similarity, and batch size.

Appendix D.1 gives a concrete counterexample (F(x) = sqrt(1-x^2)) showing that general convex constraints can destroy smoothness of the hyper-objective, which properly motivates the extra assumptions used in the general-constraint extension.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistency in the central complexity claims. Theorem 4.6 claims the oracle outputs an epsilon-accurate gradient within O(log(1/epsilon)) gradient oracle evaluations, but its proof (Theorem C.2) states 'within O~(1) gradient oracle evaluations' and never exhibits a log factor; conversely Algorithm 1 sets delta = O(epsilon) while the proof of C.2 sets delta-tilde = O(epsilon^2). The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all tout O(log(1/epsilon)) and O~(delta^-1 epsilon^-3), so this mismatch goes to the headline result.

The claimed complexity is built on an unjustified assumption about the cost of the inner solves: the proof of Theorem C.2 asserts that 'since both Problem P0 and Problem P3 are well-conditioned, we can obtain delta-tilde-close primal solutions in O~(1) time.' No solver or algorithm achieving this is given, and for black-box commercial solvers (Gurobi, MOSEK) no meaningful operation count is possible. The 'near-constant O(log(1/epsilon)) first-order information' claim therefore conflates oracle complexity of gradients with the cost of solving two optimization problems per hypergradient, which in practice dominates.

The proof of Lemma C.1 is hand-wavy at critical steps: it assumes differentiability of the perturbed primal-dual path in delta (granted via strong regularity, but not verified under the stated assumptions), uses first-order Taylor expansions with O(delta^2) remainders without bounding constants, and Equation (25) asserts lambda-tilde(x) = 0 without justification. The proof of Theorem B.1 reduces to 'simple linear algebra' comparing two KKT systems, and the reduction of Equation (15) to (14) is asserted rather than shown; the multiplier structure of the ghost problem (frozen multipliers entering the objective) deserves a rigorous perturbation argument.

The extension to general convex constraints (Appendix D, Corollary D.5) is largely by assumption: Assumption D.1.1 posits an approximate oracle that returns solutions with the correct active set and dual accuracy, which the authors admit is postulated because 'we are not aware of any algorithm that achieves linear convergence for the dual solution' in this setting. Presenting this as 'extending the guarantee to general convex-constrained settings' (a stated contribution) overstates what is proven; the results hold for a narrow 'well-behaved' class essentially by construction of the assumptions.

Assumption 4.3 (correct active-set identification) is strong and not guaranteed by the black-box solvers the method claims compatibility with; the practical consequences (e.g., near-degenerate multipliers, which the authors' own Appendix F example shows are exactly the hard case) are only partially mitigated by the randomized smoothing fallback, whose guarantee (Theorem F.2) introduces additional problem-dependent quantities (inradius rho-bar) and degrades the rate.

Evaluation is limited and largely synthetic: three benchmark tasks (synthetic DFL, Sudoku from OptNet, and a synthetic SOCP), all run on CPU, with problem sizes at most dy = 1000. There are no real-world decision-focused learning applications, and results are mixed - QPTH has a faster backward pass in all QP tasks and faster forward in Sudoku, and the headline 'significantly faster' claim rests on comparisons where CvxpyLayer's known canonicalization overhead, rather than the proposed method's core advantage, drives much of the gap. Alt-Diff is excluded because the authors found it 'too slow', weakening the baseline coverage.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: the source-code URL in the abstract is missing entirely (the sentence is cut off), Figure 8's caption contains 'epsilon = 10=12', the conclusion says 'well-clock time' instead of wall-clock, Lemma A.3's statement is incomplete (unclear norm/constant on the RHS), and there are duplicated references (Zhang et al. 2020a/2020b; Maclaurin et al. 2015a/2015b) as well as an impact-statement-adjacent reference list padded with marginally relevant citations.

The contribution sits close to Kornowski et al. (2024): the hypergradient oracle and convergence analysis follow that paper's machinery (their Lemma 3.2, Lemma A.7, and meta-algorithm are invoked directly in the proofs), with the main novelty being the active-set/ghost reduction. Given this proximity, the theoretical novelty over Kornowski et al.'s equality-constrained result is modest and hinges on proofs that, as noted above, contain gaps.

strengths: The core idea is original and well-motivated: converting inequality-constrained lower-level problems into an equality-constrained 'ghost' bilevel problem via active-set identification and linearization, thereby achieving O(log(1/ε)) hypergradient approximation where prior penalty-based approaches (Kornowski et al., 2024) require O(1/ε). This addresses a gap explicitly highlighted as open in prior work.

The theoretical contribution is layered nicely: Theorem 4.5 (active-set equivalence) justifies the reduction, Lemma C.1/Theorem 4.6 give finite-time hypergradient accuracy, and Corollary 4.7 matches the best-known O(δ⁻¹ε⁻³) Goldstein complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization—now with linearly constrained, and (under additional assumptions) general convex-constrained, bilevel problems.

The solver-agnostic reformulation (Lemma E.1, replacing δf with δc⊤y using a stop-gradient) is a clever and practically important trick that makes the method usable as a black-box layer compatible with strong commercial solvers (GUROBI, MOSEK), which most existing layers cannot do.

Appendix F is a commendable treatment of limitations: it proves the active-set assumption is necessary (Lemma F.1 gives an impossibility result for continuous estimators) and complements it with a smoothed variant (Theorem F.2) that removes the assumption at additional cost. Appendix D.1 gives an honest example showing the upper-level landscape can be non-Lipschitz under general convex constraints.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough: three tasks, multiple strong baselines, and useful ablations (memory scaling, solver-tolerance sensitivity, gradient cosine similarity against a proxy exact oracle, batch-size amortization, LPGD tolerance analysis). The released drop-in PyTorch library supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The assumptions are restrictive relative to the paper's framing. Beyond strong convexity of the lower level (which excludes many practical layers) and LICQ, Assumption 4.3 (exact active-set identification) is strong: degenerate or near-degenerate multipliers—common in practice—break correct identification, and Theorem 4.5 additionally requires the active set to be locally constant, which fails precisely near constraint transitions. While Appendix F shows some version of this is unavoidable, the gap between the clean theory and realistic regimes deserves more discussion than it receives.

The generalization to 'general convex constraints' (Appendix D) is largely assumption-driven rather than algorithmic: Assumption D.1.1 assumes an oracle returning approximate primal-dual solutions with the correct active set, and the authors state they are 'not aware of any algorithm that achieves linear convergence for the dual solution' in this setting. The resulting Corollary D.5 is therefore an oracle-complexity statement rather than an implementable guarantee, which weakens the claimed second main contribution.

The oracle-complexity claims warrant scrutiny: each 'gradient oracle evaluation' in Algorithm 1 requires solving two constrained convex programs (Lines 2–3) to ˜δ-accuracy. Comparing O(log(1/ε)) such calls against O(1/ε) penalty iterations is apples-to-oranges unless the per-call solve cost is accounted for; the near-constant claim hides the fact that the forward/backward cost is dominated by black-box solves. The experiments partially address practical cost, but the theoretical complexity comparison in Corollary 4.7 could mislead.

Several proofs are compressed to the point of being difficult to verify: Theorem B.1's proof concludes 'by simple linear algebra' for the key equivalence; Theorem C.2 relies on informal conditioning claims ('well-conditioned', 'O˜(1) time'); some bounds in Appendix A (e.g., Lemma A.3, Lemma A.4) skip steps and mix notational conventions. These should be tightened for claims central to the paper.

The experimental scale is modest: dimension up to d_y = 1000, 2-layer MLPs, synthetic DFL, Sudoku, and a synthetic SOCP. There is no real-world decision-focused application (e.g., energy, portfolio, or scheduling benchmarks), so the claimed scalability advantages are demonstrated only within a narrow synthetic regime. Also, all baselines are run on CPU due to batch-solver limitations, which may disadvantage some baselines (partially mitigated by the GPU ablation for QPTH).

The method yields only an approximate (O(δ)) hypergradient, whereas KKT-based methods provide exact gradients; Table 1 honestly marks this, but the paper does not analyze when the accumulated finite-difference bias could affect downstream training quality beyond empirical cosine-similarity plots.

Presentation issues: several typos and formatting glitches (e.g., 'well-clock time' in the conclusion, Figure 13's 'Loss vs iter' axis labels, inconsistent ϵ/ε usage, duplicated citation of Zhang et al. 2020a/b with identical pages), and the algorithmic section would benefit from stating the full per-iteration cost model explicitly.
